passages.title: The Humble Pencil
paras: A

Few objects are as ordinary as the pencil, yet its history connects a hillside in the north of England, a French engineer and a nineteenth-century marketing decision that still shapes what pencils look like today. The story begins in the mid-sixteenth century, when a large deposit of an unusually pure, solid form of graphite was found near Borrowdale in Cumbria. Local shepherds are said to have used lumps of it to mark their sheep, and before long the material was being cut into sticks for writing and drawing.
B

At first, nobody was quite sure what the substance was. Because it left a dark grey mark much like that of lead, it became known as 'black lead' or 'plumbago', and the name stuck: even now, many people talk about the 'lead' in a pencil, although pencils have never contained the metal. It was not until the late eighteenth century that chemists showed graphite to be a form of carbon.
C

The Borrowdale graphite was so valuable that the mine was guarded, and for a period it was opened for only a few weeks each year in order to keep prices high. Theft and smuggling were common, and in 1752 the British Parliament made stealing graphite a serious crime. Because the solid graphite was brittle and dirtied the fingers, users wrapped the sticks in string or sheepskin; later, craftsmen began to glue them into grooves cut in strips of wood, creating something close to the modern pencil.
D

Countries without access to high-quality graphite had to find another solution. In Germany, pencil makers in Nuremberg experimented with mixing powdered graphite with sulphur and other substances, but the results were scratchy and uneven. The decisive breakthrough came in France in 1795. With war cutting off supplies of English graphite, the engineer Nicolas-Jacques Conté developed a method of combining powdered graphite with clay, shaping the mixture into rods and firing them in a kiln. Conté's process had a further advantage: by changing the proportion of clay to graphite, manufacturers could make leads that were harder or softer, lighter or darker. This is the origin of the grading systems still printed on pencils, such as HB.
E

During the nineteenth century, pencil making became an industry. Mechanised factories in Germany and, later, the United States produced pencils in enormous quantities, and cedar became the preferred wood because it was soft enough to sharpen easily but did not split. Many manufacturers also adopted a hexagonal shape rather than a round one, partly because it used wood efficiently and partly because a six-sided pencil is less likely to roll off a sloping desk.
F

The familiar yellow colour has a more commercial explanation. In the 1890s, a European company launched a premium pencil filled with graphite from a mine in Asia and painted it bright yellow, a colour associated at the time with luxury and with the East. The pencil was a great success, and rival firms soon copied the colour so that their own products would look equally high-quality. In North America in particular, yellow is still the colour most people picture when they think of a pencil.
G

Despite the arrival of ballpoint pens and digital devices, billions of pencils are still made every year. Pencils work in very cold conditions, they do not leak, and their marks can be rubbed out, which explains why they remain popular with artists, carpenters and schoolchildren alike.

passages.title: Cooling the City
paras: A

On a still summer evening, the centre of a large city can be several degrees warmer than the surrounding countryside. This difference, known as the urban heat island effect, was first described in the early nineteenth century by the amateur scientist Luke Howard, who recorded temperatures in and around London. Since then it has been measured in cities of every size and climate, and it is generally strongest at night, when the countryside cools quickly but the city releases heat it has stored during the day.
B

Several features of cities contribute to the effect. Roads, roofs and car parks are often dark, so they absorb a large share of the sunlight that falls on them rather than reflecting it. Materials such as concrete, brick and asphalt also store heat well and give it back slowly after sunset. Tall buildings can trap warm air between them and reduce the wind that would otherwise carry heat away. In addition, cities produce heat of their own: vehicles, factories and air-conditioning units all release warmth directly into the streets.
C

The consequences are more than a matter of comfort. During heatwaves, high night-time temperatures prevent people's bodies from recovering, and studies of past heatwaves have linked hot nights to increased hospital admissions, particularly among elderly people. Higher temperatures also raise demand for electricity for cooling, which can strain power networks at exactly the moment they are needed most, and they speed up the chemical reactions that produce ground-level ozone, a pollutant that irritates the lungs.
D

One of the simplest responses is to change the colour of urban surfaces. 'Cool roofs', painted white or covered with reflective materials, can stay far cooler in direct sun than conventional dark roofs, reducing the heat passed into the rooms below. Some cities have experimented with lighter-coloured road coatings as well. However, researchers point out that reflective surfaces at street level can bounce sunlight onto pedestrians and nearby walls, so their benefits depend heavily on where they are used.
E

Vegetation offers a different kind of cooling. Trees shade streets and buildings, and like all plants they release water vapour through their leaves, a process that uses energy and therefore cools the surrounding air. Parks can be noticeably cooler than nearby built-up areas, and green roofs, covered with soil and plants, both insulate buildings and add moisture to the air. The drawbacks are mainly practical: trees take years to grow, they need water during dry periods, and green roofs can only be installed on buildings strong enough to carry their weight.
F

Experts increasingly argue that no single measure will be enough and that cooling must be built into planning from the start. This may mean designing streets so that wind can flow along them, protecting existing green spaces, or setting rules for the materials used in new buildings. As summers in many regions become hotter, the question is no longer whether cities should adapt, but how quickly they can do so.

passages.title: Too Much Choice?
paras: A

In a now-famous experiment carried out in a Californian supermarket, the psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting stand offering shoppers samples of jam. On some days the stand displayed twenty-four varieties; on others, just six. The larger display attracted more visitors, but when it came to buying, the result was striking: about 30 per cent of the people who stopped at the small display went on to buy a jar, compared with only around 3 per cent of those who had seen the large one. The study, published in 2000, seemed to show that more choice could actually make people less likely to choose at all.
B

The finding captured the public imagination. It fitted a growing unease about modern consumer life, in which supermarkets stock tens of thousands of products and online shops offer almost unlimited options. The psychologist Barry Schwartz popularised the idea in a widely read book, arguing that an abundance of choice could leave people anxious, prone to regret and less satisfied with what they eventually selected. 'Choice overload' became a familiar term in business schools, and some companies reduced the number of products they sold in the hope of increasing sales.
C

Researchers, however, soon began to ask how general the effect really was. When later studies tried to repeat the jam experiment and similar ones with other products, the results were mixed: some found that large assortments reduced buying, some found no difference, and some found that more options actually helped. In 2010 a team led by Benjamin Scheibehenne combined the results of dozens of such experiments in a single statistical analysis, and concluded that, on average, the effect of the number of options was close to zero.
D

This did not mean that choice overload was imaginary. Instead, attention turned to the conditions under which it appears. A later review, published in 2015, suggested that people are more likely to struggle when the decision is difficult in itself – for example, when the options are hard to compare – when they have no clear preference in advance, when the choice must be made quickly, or when they are trying to find the single best option rather than one that is simply good enough. In other circumstances, a large range may be welcomed, particularly by people who already know what they want.
E

These findings have practical implications. Organisations that offer complex products, such as pension plans, have found that providing a sensible default option, which people receive unless they actively choose something else, can help those who would otherwise put off deciding altogether. Grouping options into clear categories, or providing tools that let people narrow down a list according to what matters to them, can also make large ranges easier to handle.
F

The story of choice overload also illustrates how science works. A single striking result can travel far beyond the laboratory, especially when it confirms what many people already suspect. Yet the real picture usually emerges only when many studies are compared, and it is often more complicated than the first headline suggested.

passages.title: A Brief History of Tea
paras: A

Tea is now drunk in almost every country in the world, but for most of its history it was a Chinese drink. According to legend, its properties were discovered thousands of years ago, when leaves from a wild tea bush blew into a pot of water being boiled for an emperor. Whatever the truth of the story, there is good evidence that people in south-western China were using tea leaves well over two thousand years ago, at first mainly as a medicine and as an ingredient in food rather than as an everyday drink.
B

By the time of the Tang dynasty, which ruled China from the seventh to the tenth century, tea drinking had become a widespread custom. In the eighth century the writer Lu Yu produced 'The Classic of Tea', a detailed guide to growing, preparing and serving it, which helped to turn tea into a symbol of refinement. At this time tea was usually pressed into hard cakes, which were broken up, ground into powder and whisked with hot water. The practice of steeping loose leaves in water, which is how most tea is prepared today, became common in China only several centuries later.
C

Tea reached Europe at the beginning of the seventeenth century, carried by Dutch traders who bought it in Asian ports. At first it was an expensive novelty, sold in small quantities by merchants who also dealt in spices and medicines. In England it became fashionable after 1662, when the Portuguese princess Catherine of Braganza married King Charles II. She had grown up drinking tea, and her habit was soon copied by wealthy families at court.
D

For more than a century, however, tea in Britain remained heavily taxed. At times the duty amounted to more than the price of the tea itself, and a large illegal trade grew up: smugglers brought tea in from the Netherlands and other countries, and dishonest dealers stretched their supplies by mixing in leaves from other plants. The situation changed in 1784, when the government sharply reduced the tax on tea. Smuggling quickly became unprofitable, legal imports rose, and tea began its transformation into the national drink of Britain.
E

Until the nineteenth century, almost all the tea drunk in Europe came from China. Concerned about depending on a single supplier, the British East India Company encouraged experiments in growing tea in its Indian territories. In the 1830s a variety of the tea plant that grew naturally in the region of Assam, in north-east India, was recognised as suitable for commercial production, and the first plantations were established. Within a few decades, tea from India, and later from Ceylon, now Sri Lanka, was being exported in large quantities, and the price of tea fell further.
F

The twentieth century brought another change in the way tea was prepared. Tea bags are said to have been invented almost by accident in the United States in the early 1900s, when a merchant sent samples of tea to customers in small silk bags, and some of them put the bags directly into hot water. Whether or not this story is accurate, tea bags became popular because they were quick and tidy to use. Today they account for the great majority of the tea sold in Britain, while many tea drinkers in other parts of the world continue to prefer loose leaves.

passages.title: Sleep and Memory
paras: A

For a long time, sleep was regarded as a passive state, a time when the brain simply switched off to rest. Research over the past few decades has overturned this view. While we sleep, the brain passes through a regular cycle of stages, and during some of them it is at least as active as when we are awake. Increasingly, scientists believe that one of the main purposes of this activity is to process and store the experiences of the day.
B

Sleep is usually divided into rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, when most vivid dreaming takes place, and non-REM sleep, which includes the deepest stage, known as slow-wave sleep. In a typical night, an adult goes through four or five cycles, each lasting about ninety minutes. Slow-wave sleep is concentrated in the early part of the night, while REM periods become longer towards the morning. This pattern matters, because different stages appear to support different kinds of memory.
C

Some of the most striking evidence has come from studies of animals. In the 1990s, researchers recording the activity of individual nerve cells in the hippocampus of rats, a brain area involved in memory for places, found that the same sequences of activity that occurred while the animals explored a maze were repeated while they slept afterwards. This 'replay' is thought to strengthen the memory, gradually transferring information to other parts of the brain for long-term storage.
D

Experiments with people point in the same direction. In a common design, volunteers learn a list of word pairs or a set of facts in the evening and are tested the next morning; their results are compared with those of volunteers who learn the same material in the morning and are tested in the evening, after a day awake. Those who have slept usually remember more. Slow-wave sleep seems particularly important for facts and events, while REM sleep has been linked to emotional memories and to skills, such as playing a melody on a keyboard.
E

Sleep before learning also matters. When people are deprived of a night's sleep and then asked to learn new information, they perform considerably worse than well-rested people, suggesting that a tired brain is less able to take in new memories in the first place. On the positive side, even a short daytime nap can improve performance on some memory tasks, which has led some researchers to argue that schools and workplaces should take rest more seriously.
F

Many questions remain. It is not yet clear exactly how the brain decides which memories to keep and which to discard, or why some people seem to need much less sleep than others. Researchers are also cautious about popular claims that people can learn new skills, such as a foreign language, simply by listening to recordings while they sleep; there is little evidence that this works for complex material. What is clear is that sleep is not wasted time, but an active part of how we learn.

passages.title: The Rise of Citizen Science
paras: A

Every winter since 1900, thousands of volunteers in North America have spent a day counting birds. The Christmas Bird Count was proposed by the ornithologist Frank Chapman as an alternative to a holiday tradition of shooting birds, and it has since grown into one of the longest-running wildlife surveys in the world. Its records have helped scientists track changes in the populations and ranges of hundreds of species over more than a century. It is also an early example of what is now called citizen science: research in which members of the public, most of them without scientific training, collect or analyse data.
B

For most of the twentieth century, such projects were limited by practical problems. Volunteers had to be in the right place at the right time, and their observations had to be posted on paper and entered by hand. The internet changed this. Since the early 2000s, online projects have allowed people anywhere in the world to contribute from their own homes, and the number of participants has grown enormously.
C

One of the best-known examples is Galaxy Zoo, launched in 2007 by astronomers who faced a problem: a telescope survey had produced images of around a million galaxies, far too many for a small team to classify by eye, and computers of the time could not reliably tell the main shapes apart. The team invited the public to help, expecting a modest response. Instead, within a year, volunteers had made tens of millions of classifications. One volunteer, a Dutch schoolteacher, even noticed a strange glowing object that professional astronomers had not described, which became the subject of further research.
D

Other projects ask volunteers to solve problems rather than simply sort data. In the online game Foldit, players manipulate digital models of proteins, trying to find the shapes that require the least energy. In 2011, players produced a model of an enzyme from a virus related to HIV, a structure that scientists had struggled to determine for many years. The players' solution, reached within weeks, was later confirmed by researchers, and they were credited as co-authors of the scientific paper describing it.
E

Not all scientists are convinced. The most common concern is the quality of the data: volunteers may make mistakes, identify species wrongly or record observations inconsistently. Project designers have responded in several ways. Many projects show the same image to several volunteers and combine their answers, so that individual errors cancel out; others compare volunteers' results with those of experts, or provide training and tests before people can take part. Studies of well-designed projects have found that the combined judgements of volunteers can be as accurate as those of professionals.
F

In my view, the benefits of citizen science go beyond the data it produces. Participants often report that they learn a great deal and feel a stronger connection to nature or to science. At a time when public trust in experts is often said to be declining, projects that invite people to take part in real research may be one of the best ways of showing how science actually works. Citizen science will not replace professional research, but it has become a valuable partner.

passages.title: The Lunchbox Carriers of Mumbai
paras: A

Every working day in Mumbai, India's largest city, around two hundred thousand home-cooked lunches travel from kitchens in the suburbs to offices in the city centre, and then back again in the afternoon. They are carried by the dabbawalas, a word that roughly means 'those who carry boxes'. The service began in 1890, when a man named Mahadeo Havaji Bachche started delivering lunches to office workers who preferred food prepared at home to what was available near their workplaces.
B

Today around five thousand dabbawalas work in the system. Each morning, a dabbawala collects lunchboxes from homes in his area, usually by bicycle, and takes them to the nearest railway station. There the boxes are sorted according to their destination and loaded onto the city's suburban trains. At stations in the city centre they are sorted again and delivered by other members of the team, often carried on long wooden crates or pushed on handcarts through crowded streets. In the afternoon, the whole process runs in reverse, and the empty boxes are returned home.
C

What makes the system remarkable is that it relies almost entirely on people rather than technology. Many dabbawalas have had only a few years of formal education, so instead of written addresses, each lunchbox is marked with a simple code of coloured symbols, letters and numbers. The code shows the area where the box was collected, the station it must travel to, and the building and floor where it should be delivered. A single box may pass through the hands of three or four different dabbawalas during its journey.
D

The service has attracted attention far beyond India. A frequently repeated claim, which appeared in a business magazine in the late 1990s, is that the dabbawalas make only one mistake in every sixteen million deliveries. Some researchers have since questioned how this figure was calculated, but there is general agreement that errors are very rare. Business schools have studied the system as an example of efficient organisation, and visitors, including members of the British royal family, have come to see it in action.
E

Researchers who have studied the dabbawalas point to several reasons for their success. The work is organised in small groups of about twenty people, each responsible for its own area and finances, and every member is a shareholder in the organisation rather than an employee. The rules are strict: dabbawalas must wear a white cap at work, are fined for being late, and are not allowed to drink alcohol during working hours. Perhaps most importantly, the system is simple, so each person knows exactly what is expected of them.
F

The dabbawalas have faced challenges in recent years. Some offices now provide canteens, food delivery apps offer alternatives, and during the Covid-19 pandemic, when most offices closed, the service almost stopped completely. Even so, the organisation has adapted, for example by allowing customers to book through a mobile app, and for many families in Mumbai a home-cooked lunch delivered to the office remains part of daily life.

passages.title: Swarms on the Move
paras: A

For most of the time, the desert locust is an unremarkable insect. It lives alone in the dry regions that stretch from West Africa to India, avoids other locusts, and is coloured to blend in with sand and stones. Yet under certain conditions this solitary grasshopper changes dramatically in appearance and behaviour, joining with millions of others to form swarms that can strip crops from vast areas of land. Few natural events have caused as much fear among farmers throughout history.
B

The change is triggered by crowding. After heavy rain, plants grow quickly in the desert and locusts breed in large numbers. When the vegetation then dries out, the insects are forced together in the remaining green areas. Experiments have shown that repeated touching of the hind legs, which happens when locusts are packed closely together, is enough to start the transformation. Within a few hours their behaviour changes: instead of avoiding each other, they are attracted to other locusts. Over several generations, their colour also changes from dull brown to bright yellow and black, and their bodies alter in shape.
C

Once they have reached this 'gregarious' phase, young locusts, which cannot yet fly, march across the ground in bands. Adult locusts form flying swarms that may cover hundreds of square kilometres and contain tens of millions of insects in every square kilometre. Carried by the wind, a swarm can travel well over a hundred kilometres in a day, and swarms have occasionally crossed the Atlantic Ocean. Because each locust eats roughly its own weight in fresh food every day, even a small swarm can consume as much food in a day as thousands of people.
D

Controlling locusts has always been difficult because outbreaks begin in remote areas that are hard to monitor. Today, an international warning system run by the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization collects reports from national teams, satellite data on rainfall and vegetation, and weather forecasts in order to predict where swarms are likely to form. When an outbreak is detected early, teams can spray the affected areas before swarms develop. Once large swarms are on the move, control is far more expensive and less effective.
E

The importance of early warning was shown between 2019 and 2021, when unusual cyclones brought heavy rain to the Arabian Peninsula. Swarms formed in areas where monitoring was limited by conflict, and spread into East Africa and South Asia, causing the worst outbreak in some countries for several decades. A large international response, including extensive spraying from aircraft, eventually brought the situation under control, but not before significant damage had been done to crops and pasture.
F

Researchers are now looking for methods that cause less harm to the environment than chemical pesticides. One promising approach uses a fungus that attacks locusts but not other insects; it acts more slowly than chemicals but is considered much safer. Others are studying the signals that cause locusts to gather, hoping that one day it may be possible to interrupt the process before swarms begin to form.

passages.title: Why Do We Put Things Off?
paras: A

Almost everyone procrastinates at times, delaying a task they intend to do even though they expect to be worse off for the delay. Surveys suggest that a large proportion of university students consider themselves regular procrastinators, and that the habit is common among adults too. For a long time, procrastination was treated as a problem of time management: if people simply planned their days better, the thinking went, they would get things done. Researchers now believe this explanation misses something important.
B

According to a view that has become influential over the past two decades, procrastination is mainly a problem of managing emotions rather than time. A task that makes us feel bored, anxious or uncertain produces an unpleasant mood, and putting it off provides immediate relief. The relief is short-lived, and the task usually becomes more stressful as the deadline approaches, but because the reward of avoiding it comes straight away, the habit is easily reinforced. Seen in this way, procrastinators are not lazy; they are trying, in an unhelpful way, to feel better.
C

This also helps to explain why people delay even tasks they consider important. Psychologists have long observed that humans tend to value immediate rewards more highly than future ones, a tendency sometimes called 'present bias'. The benefits of finishing an essay or completing a tax return lie in the future, while the discomfort of starting is felt now. Some researchers describe the situation as a conflict between our present self and our future self, whom we often treat almost as a stranger.
D

If procrastination is about emotions, then simply telling people to try harder is unlikely to work, and may even make things worse. One much-cited study followed university students through two sets of exams. Students who said that they had forgiven themselves for putting off revision for the first exams procrastinated less before the second set than those who had been hard on themselves. The researchers suggested that self-criticism added to the negative feelings associated with studying, making avoidance more likely.
E

Practical strategies based on this research focus on making it easier to start. Breaking a large task into very small steps reduces the uncertainty that often triggers avoidance. Another technique is to form what psychologists call an 'implementation intention', a specific plan stating when and where an action will be taken, for example: 'At nine o'clock tomorrow, in the library, I will write the first paragraph.' Studies have found that plans of this kind increase the chances that people actually carry out their intentions.
F

None of this means that every delay is harmful. Waiting for more information before making a decision can be sensible, and some people claim that they work best under the pressure of a deadline. Yet research on students generally finds that those who procrastinate most tend to experience more stress and, on average, achieve lower grades. Understanding the emotional roots of the habit may be the most useful first step towards changing it.
